points.t: Possession of the whole farm sought against Frederick Buckler alone, summary judgment, no trial
points.what: Possession of the whole farm was sought against Frederick Buckler alone and obtained under Order 14, the summary procedure, without a trial.
points.quote: Western Ground Rents then brought proceedings for possession against Mr Frederick Buckler in the High Court and obtained a possession order, under Order 14, in respect of the whole of the farm.
points.why: Mary (Nancy) Williams lived in the farmhouse and was not a party. The order that started the chain was made with no hearing of the person whose home it was, and the house was left out of the enforcement on 4 July 1955 because of her.

points.t: “The whole of the farm”: no parcel or plan identified
points.what: The 1955 order is recited as covering “the whole of the farm”, and the 1916 letting as of “the whole of the farm”. No plan or parcel list is quoted for either.
points.quote: possession was taken in respect of all parts of the farm except the farmhouse and garden
points.why: The land each order bound is described only as “the whole” or by exclusion. The appeal was limited to the farmhouse and garden “shown coloured red on the plan served with the statement of claim” (¶2); that plan is not reproduced in the judgment.

points.t: 1962 order left unenforced for almost twelve years, then revived by a successor
points.what: A possession order for the farmhouse and garden was made on 11 December 1962 and then left unenforced for almost twelve years.
points.quote: nothing was done before 1974 to enforce the 1962 possession order
points.why: The order was revived in September 1974, less than three months before its twelve years ran out, by a company that was not the party it was made for. The Court of Appeal later held it kept the owner’s title alive to 31 October 1974.

points.t: The occupier’s 1974 defence filed and never heard
points.what: BP Pension Trust’s own possession action was adjourned part heard for a defence. The defence pleaded that the claim was barred by adverse possession under the Limitation Act 1939.
points.quote: That action has never been finally heard.
points.why: The occupier’s pleaded defence was never decided in the action brought against her. The owner moved instead to enforce the 1962 order, and her defence stayed on the court file, unheard, until her death in March 1983.

points.t: Leave to enforce granted on two days’ notice while the owner’s own action was part heard
points.what: Notice of an application for leave to enforce the 1962 order was given on 17 September 1974; leave was granted on 19 September, two days later, to BP Pension Trust “as successors in title to Western Ground Rents”.
points.quote: on the ground that Mrs Buckler had had insufficient notice of the application and therefore had had no opportunity of presenting her case
points.why: Two days’ notice, while the applicant’s own action against her was part heard. The ground of her appeal, recorded in the judgment, is the want of a hearing.

points.t: Succession to the 1962 order rests on a conveyance missing from both registration files
points.what: Leave to enforce the 1962 order was given to BP Pension Trust as “successors in title to Western Ground Rents”, and the Court of Appeal held the order still enforceable by “the landlords” on 31 October 1974.
points.quote: enforcement of the judgment for possession of December 11 1962 was still open to the landlords at October 31 1974
points.why: The succession rests on the December 1969 sale, recited in the judgment. That conveyance is not listed on either HM Land Registry first-registration file.

points.t: Appeal for want of notice never heard
points.what: The occupier’s solicitors issued a notice of appeal against the leave order, on the ground of insufficient notice, and booked a stay hearing for 4 November.
points.why: The judgment records the notice of appeal and no hearing of it. The warrant was withdrawn before 25 November 1974, so the complaint that she had no chance to present her case was never decided by any court.

points.t: The letters went to her solicitor, arriving the morning of the hearing
points.what: The two letters of 31 October 1974 were addressed to the occupier but sent to her solicitor, who received them on the morning of 4 November, immediately before the stay hearing. The owner’s solicitors did not attend.
points.quote: both were in fact sent not to her but to her solicitor, who seems to have received them on the morning of November 4
points.why: The documents that later decided the case reached the court, not the person they bound, four days after the warrant became enforceable (31 October, ¶11). She had not seen them before the hearing they were produced at.

points.t: Stay pending her agreement; warrant withdrawn before she could answer
points.what: The judge stayed execution pending the occupier’s agreement to the proposals in the letters. Before she had given instructions, the owner’s solicitors withdrew the warrant.
points.quote: Before she had given any instructions, however, the landlords’ solicitors themselves wrote to the county court, at some date prior to November 25 1974 and withdrew the warrant for possession.
points.why: The court set her agreement as the next step. The owner then removed the step, so her answer was never asked for, and the 1987 court treated the silence that followed as acceptance of a licence.

points.what: The farmhouse and garden were first registered (WA240304) on an application lodged by the owner’s solicitors (Form 1C), while the 1974 action, with the occupier’s pleaded defence, stood unheard.
points.quote: (11) Form 1C application form from Linklaters & Paines

points.t: 1984 writ against her son after her death; her estate never represented
points.what: BP Properties Ltd issued a writ for possession against William Buckler, fourteen months after his mother’s death. No grant of representation to her estate was ever obtained.
points.quote: In fact no grant of representation to the estate of Mrs Buckler has so far been obtained
points.why: Her possession was the issue the case turned on, yet she was dead and her estate was not represented. The person whose acts and silences were judged could not give evidence, and her own 1974 defence was never heard.

points.forum: High Court, Queen’s Bench Division, Cardiff
points.t: Trial judge’s adverse-possession finding reversed as wrong on appeal
points.what: The trial judge held Frederick Buckler was not in adverse possession and that the occupier’s own intention could count for nothing while her husband lived.
points.quote: The judge then held - paradoxically, in my view, on the facts of this case - that he could not give any effect to Mrs Buckler’s obvious animus possidendi while her husband was alive
points.why: The Court of Appeal held “without hesitation” that both were in adverse possession from 2 February 1955 (¶23): the trial finding was wrong. The appeal still failed on the enforcement and licence points, so the error never changed the outcome.

points.t: A rule the court called new, applied to 1974 conduct
points.what: The court applied a rule it described as new: that a licence granted by one side alone stops the limitation clock.
points.quote: The claim that a unilateral licence can stop time running is a new one.
points.why: The rule was first stated in 1987 and applied to conduct in 1974 by an occupier who died in 1983. The court itself noted it would let an owner avoid enforcing a possession order and keep title alive “until it suits him to evict” (¶32).

points.t: Bound by letters whose acceptance was never sought
points.what: The court found the occupier was bound by the letters though BP Properties never asked for her acceptance.
points.quote: BP Properties Ltd neither sought nor waited for her acceptance.
points.why: The burden of answering was placed on a person who was never asked. Silence from someone who was not asked is not the same as consent.

points.t: “In the absence of any repudiation”: her pleaded defence stood on the court file
points.what: The decisive finding: the occupier was a licensee “in the absence of any repudiation” of the 31 October 1974 letters, and was not asserting any claim to ownership after them.
points.quote: In essence she was not asserting during the time from the receipt of the letters until after December 11 1974 - or indeed thereafter - any claim to ownership of the farmhouse and garden
points.why: The same judgment records that her defence in the 1974 action, pleading that the owner’s claim was barred, was filed and “has never been finally heard” (¶11). A pleading asserting her title stood on the court file throughout. The judgment also records that she did nothing on her solicitors’ advice to wait for the twelve years from the 1962 order to expire (¶34); that advice was then counted as acceptance.

points.t: “Had agreed to buy” taken from the letters alone; conveyance 23 May 1975
points.what: The “wrong company” argument was answered from the letters’ own words that BP Properties Ltd “had agreed to buy”. No agreement was before the court; the conveyance to BP Properties is dated 23 May 1975.
points.quote: the letters record sufficiently that BP Properties Ltd had agreed to buy the property from the Pension Trust
points.why: HM Land Registry’s file lists a plan to the conveyance dated 23 February 1975, almost four months after the letters. The existence of a binding agreement on 31 October 1974 rests on the letters alone.

points.t: “Registered … in November 1982”: the farmhouse title dates from 23 Feb 1983
points.what: The court recorded BP Properties as registered proprietor “of the whole of the farm” since November 1982.
points.quote: BP Properties Ltd were registered as the proprietors of the whole of the farm at HM Land Registry in November 1982
points.why: HM Land Registry dates the application for the farm (WA231076) 30 November 1982, but the farmhouse and garden were registered separately (WA240304, register edition 23 February 1983, Form 1C). The two titles were merged on 2 February 1987. The 1987 wording matches the register as merged in February 1987, not the register as it stood in November 1982.

points.t: Frederick Buckler’s death left as “1965-67”; the GRO index gives 1967
points.what: The date of Frederick Buckler’s death was left as “some time in the period 1965-67”, though the limitation period ran from it.

points.forum: Bailiffs; European Commission of Human Rights
points.t: Possession and demolition while the Strasbourg application was pending
points.what: Possession was taken on 29 November 1988 and demolition of the farmhouse began on 6 December, while the application to Strasbourg, lodged on 3 May 1988, was pending.
points.quote: On 29 November 1988 the company obtained possession of the property and on 6 December demolition of the farmhouse began.
points.why: The subject of the complaint was destroyed before the Commission decided it (14 April 1989). Whatever the outcome, no remedy could restore the house.

points.t: Not listed on 5 Dec 1988; demolition began the next day; no reasons produced
points.what: Cadw decided not to list the farmhouse on 5 December 1988, after a listing inspection on 29 July 1988. Demolition began the next day.
points.quote: did not meet the listing criteria
points.why: Cadw’s 2026 reply gives the result and two inspection photographs. No assessment, reasons or site notes for the decision have been produced.
